topics.name: Multi-Agent Patterns and Trade-offs
topics.description: Choosing between subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflows.
notes: ## 为什么需要 multi-agent
- 三大诉求：context management（按需提供专业知识）、distributed development（团队独立维护）、parallelization（并行子任务）。
- 并非所有复杂任务都需要多 agent：配备合适（甚至动态）tools 和 prompt 的单 agent 往往已足够。
- 多 agent 设计的核心是 context engineering：决定每个 agent 能看到什么信息。
## 五种模式
- Subagents：主 agent 把子 agent 当作 tools 调用，所有路由经过主 agent。
- Handoffs：tools 更新 state 变量（如 current_step / active_agent），触发路由或配置切换。
- Skills：单个 agent 按需加载专门的 prompt 与知识（progressive disclosure）。
- Router：路由步骤对输入分类，分发到一个或多个 agent，再合成结果。
- Custom workflow：用 LangGraph 自定义流程，混合确定性逻辑与 agent。
## 性能对比（官方示例）
- 单次请求 'Buy coffee'：Subagents 4 次模型调用，Handoffs / Skills / Router 各 3 次（Subagents 多一次是因为结果要回到主 agent）。
- 重复请求：Handoffs 与 Skills 第二轮只需 2 次（状态或已加载的 skill 仍在）；Subagents 与 Router 无状态，每次重复完整流程。
- 多领域对比（每个领域约 2000 tokens）：Subagents 5 次约 9K tokens；Router 5 次约 9K；Skills 3 次约 15K；Handoffs 7+ 次约 14K+（顺序执行）。
- 并行执行与大上下文领域适合 Subagents / Router；Skills 适合简单、聚焦的任务。
- 模式可以混合使用，例如 Subagents 中的子 agent 也可以使用 Skills。

topics.name: Subagents as Tools
topics.description: Wrapping agents as tools: isolation, inputs, outputs, sync vs async and forking.
notes: ## Subagents 作为 tools
- 主 agent（supervisor）通过调用 tools 来协调子 agent，决定调用哪个、传什么输入、如何合并结果。
- 子 agent 默认无状态：每次调用都在干净的 context window 中运行，避免主对话的 context 膨胀。
- 子 agent 把结果返回给主 agent，而不是直接回复用户；需要用户交互时可在子 agent 内使用 interrupt。
- 主 agent 可以在一个 turn 内调用多个子 agent（并行执行）。
```python
@tool("research", description="Research a topic")
def call_research_agent(query: str):
result = subagent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": query}]})
return result["messages"][-1].content
## 设计选择
- Tool per agent：每个子 agent 一个 tool，对输入输出控制更细。
- Single dispatch tool：一个 task(agent_name, description) tool，适合 agent 多、团队分布式开发。
- 子 agent 的 name 和 description 是主 agent 选择它的主要依据；agent 超过 10 个时可用 list_agents 做 tool-based discovery。
- 输入：只传任务描述 = 隔离；传 runtime.state["messages"] = 带上父级历史。
- 输出：子 agent 的 final message 是主 agent 唯一看到的内容，要在 prompt 里要求写入结果；也可用 Command 同时回传 state key。
- Sync：主 agent 等待结果；Async：启动 job、查询状态、取结果（三 tool 模式）。
- Deep Agents：通过 task tool 委派；mode 为 isolated（默认）或 fork（继承父级对话历史，且不能再调用 task）。
- 子 agent 在 tool 内被调用时，get_state(subgraphs=True) 看不到其状态。

topics.name: Handoff Context Correctness
topics.description: ToolMessage pairing, Command.PARENT and context filtering when agents hand off.
notes: ## Handoffs 的 context 正确性
- Handoff tool 返回 Command 更新 state（如 current_step / active_agent），触发行为切换。
- LLM 调用 tool 后期望得到响应：必须有 tool_call_id 匹配的 ToolMessage，否则对话历史格式不合法。
```python
return Command(
goto="sales_agent",
update={
"active_agent": "sales_agent",
"messages": [last_ai_message, transfer_message],
graph=Command.PARENT,
- 使用 Command.PARENT 在子图 agent 之间交接时，要同时传：触发交接的 AIMessage + 确认交接的 ToolMessage。
- 不要传整个子 agent 的消息历史：会引入无关推理、增加 token；需要更多上下文时在 ToolMessage 内容里写摘要。
- 把控制权还给用户时，最后一条消息应是 AIMessage。
## 实现方式
- Single agent + middleware：用 wrap_model_call 按 current_step 覆盖 system prompt 和 tools，多数场景更简单。
- Multiple agent subgraphs：每个 agent 是图中的节点，需要精细的 context engineering；适合复杂的定制 agent。
- 设计时考虑：context 过滤策略、tool 语义（只更新路由还是带副作用）、token 效率。

topics.name: Router, Custom Workflows and Subgraphs
topics.description: Router with Send, custom LangGraph workflows and subgraph persistence modes.
notes: ## Router
- Router 对输入分类，把请求分发给一个或多个专门 agent（零个或多个并行），再把结果合成。
- 单个 agent 用 Command(goto=...)；并行扇出到多个 agent 用 Send。
```python
def route_query(state: State):
classifications = classify_query(state["query"])
return [Send(c["agent"], {"query": c["query"]}) for c in classifications]
- Stateless router：每次请求独立路由；有状态需求时最简单的做法是把 router 包成 tool，交给对话 agent 管理记忆。
- 与 supervisor 的区别：router 通常是单次分类步骤，不维护多轮对话；supervisor 是完整 agent，跨多轮动态决策。
## Custom workflow 与 subgraph
- Custom workflow 用 LangGraph 完全控制图结构：顺序、条件、循环、并行；节点可以是函数、LLM 调用或完整 agent。
- 子图与父图共享 state key：直接把编译后的子图传给 add_node；schema 不同：在节点函数里调用子图并转换状态。
## 子图持久化（checkpointer）
- None（默认，per-invocation）：每次调用从头开始，仍支持 interrupt。
- True（per-thread）：跨调用累积记忆；不支持对同一子图的并行调用。
- False（stateless）：像普通函数调用，无 interrupt、无 durable execution。
- 父图必须带 checkpointer，子图持久化功能才可用。

questions.title: In which multi-agent pattern does a single agent stay in control while loading specialized prompts and knowledge on demand?

options.text: Router
Skills
Handoffs
Subagents

questions.explanation: The skills pattern keeps one agent in control and loads specialized prompts through progressive disclosure. Subagents instead delegate work to separate agents called as tools.

questions.title: Which capabilities does the multi-agent overview list as the usual reasons developers look for multi-agent patterns?

options.text: Context management
Distributed development
Parallelization
Guaranteed lower cost than a single agent
Removing the need for tools

questions.explanation: The docs name context management, distributed development and parallelization. They also note that a single agent with the right tools and prompt can often achieve similar results, so multi-agent is not automatically cheaper.

questions.title: In the one-shot 'Buy coffee' comparison, subagents need 4 model calls while handoffs, skills and router need 3. Why does subagents need one more?

options.text: A separate routing model must classify the request first
Each subagent reloads its skill prompt before acting
Results flow back through the main agent, which adds one extra call
Subagents cannot call tools directly

questions.explanation: The docs say subagents adds one extra call because results return through the main agent, and that this overhead buys centralized control.

questions.title: On the repeat request ('Buy coffee again'), handoffs and skills need only 2 model calls on turn 2. Why?

options.text: They cache the final answer and skip the model entirely
They run the tool without any model call
They route through a stateless LLM router before acting
The active agent or loaded skill context persists, so no handoff or reload is needed

questions.explanation: Handoffs keep the coffee agent active in state and skills keep the skill in conversation history. Subagents and router are stateless and repeat the full flow.

questions.title: For 'Compare Python, JavaScript, and Rust for web development' (each domain about 2000 tokens of docs), which pattern does the overview call inefficient, and why?

options.text: Subagents, because each subagent shares the main agent's full context
Handoffs, because it runs sequentially and cannot consult the three domains in parallel
Router, because it cannot invoke agents in parallel
Skills, because it needs more than 7 model calls

questions.explanation: Handoffs needs 7+ calls and about 14K+ tokens because it executes sequentially with growing history. Skills uses only 3 calls, and subagents and router run in parallel.

questions.title: Which statements match the multi-domain comparison results in the multi-agent overview?

options.text: Subagents uses about 9K tokens because each subagent works in isolation with only its relevant context
Skills makes only 3 calls but about 15K tokens, because loaded skill docs are reprocessed on every later call
Router uses an LLM for routing and then invokes the agents in parallel, for about 9K tokens
Handoffs is the cheapest at about 5K tokens

questions.explanation: Isolation keeps subagents and router near 9K tokens, while skills accumulates context. Handoffs is the least efficient here at 7+ calls and about 14K+ tokens.

questions.title: What does the main agent receive when it calls the research tool?

options.text: The subagent's full message history
Only the content of the subagent's final message
The list of tool calls the subagent made
Nothing, because the subagent replies to the user directly

questions.explanation: The tool returns result["messages"][-1].content, so only the final message flows back to the main agent. This is what gives each subagent call context isolation.

questions.title: Fill the blank so the subagent is seeded with the parent's prior messages instead of only the task description.

options.text: [{"role": "user", "content": query}]
query
runtime.state["messages"]

questions.explanation: Passing the parent's message history seeds the subagent with prior work. Passing only the query keeps it isolated but forces it to re-derive what the parent already did.

questions.title: The main agent keeps saying the research tool returned no findings, even though the subagent ran several searches. What is the bug?

options.text: The subagent's final message is all the main agent sees, so the prompt must make it include the findings
invoke must be replaced with ainvoke
Subagents are not allowed to use tools such as web_search
The research tool needs checkpointer=True

questions.explanation: The docs warn that a subagent may do tool calls but omit results from its final message, while the supervisor only sees that final output. Here the prompt tells it to reply only 'Done.'.

questions.title: Which statements about synchronous vs asynchronous subagent execution are correct?

options.text: In a synchronous call the main agent waits for the subagent to finish before continuing
The asynchronous approach uses a start-job, check-status and get-result tool trio
Async here means the subagent must be written with Python async/await
Sync fits cases where the main agent's next action depends on the subagent's result
Async subagents block the conversation until the job completes

questions.explanation: Async means the main agent starts a background job and stays responsive, which is not the same as Python async/await. Blocking the conversation is the drawback of sync.

questions.title: A subagent compiled with checkpointer=True (per-thread persistence) is wrapped as a tool, and the model calls it twice in parallel. What do the subgraph docs warn about?

options.text: Each call gets its own checkpoint namespace, so parallel calls are safe
LangGraph silently drops the second call
Both calls write to the same namespace and cause checkpoint conflicts, so parallel calls must be prevented
Interrupts stop working, so checkpointer=False is required

questions.explanation: Per-thread subgraphs do not support parallel tool calls. The docs prevent this with ToolCallLimitMiddleware or by disabling parallel tool calling, whereas the default per-invocation mode runs safely in parallel.

questions.title: What does this subagent tool return to the parent graph?

options.text: A Command that writes the subagent's report key into the parent state and answers the tool call with a ToolMessage holding the final text
A plain string with the subagent's final message
A Command that routes to another node with goto
A Command that replaces the parent's whole message history with the subagent's messages

questions.explanation: Formatting output in code lets you pass extra state keys back besides the final text. The ToolMessage with the injected tool_call_id keeps the tool-call pairing valid.

questions.title: Why does get_state(config, subgraphs=True) not return state for a subagent invoked inside a tool function, and what do the docs suggest if you need it?

options.text: LangGraph cannot statically discover it, so invoke the subagent from a node function in a custom graph
Subagents always use checkpointer=False, so switch them to True
Subagents lack a messages key, so switch to MessagesState
Interrupts cannot propagate out of tools, so use Send instead

questions.explanation: Viewing subgraph state needs the subgraph to be statically discoverable, as a node or called inside a node. Calls hidden inside tools, as in the subagents pattern, are not.

questions.title: Which statements about Deep Agents subagent context modes are correct?

options.text: A forked subagent receives the parent's conversation history plus the delegated task
The default mode is isolated, where the subagent sees only the delegated task
A forked subagent can still call the task tool to delegate further
Isolated custom subagents inherit the parent's system prompt automatically

questions.explanation: Isolated is the default and requires its own system prompt, while fork inherits the parent's history. A fork cannot use task and must finish the work itself.

questions.title: After this handoff, the receiving agent sees a tool call with no matching response and behaves erratically. What should be added?

options.text: A messages update with the AIMessage that made the tool call and a ToolMessage using runtime.tool_call_id
Replace goto with END
Remove graph=Command.PARENT
Pass the entire subagent message history in update

questions.explanation: With Command.PARENT the docs require both the triggering AIMessage and a ToolMessage acknowledging the handoff. Passing the whole subagent history is discouraged because it adds irrelevant reasoning and tokens.

questions.title: Fill the blank so the handoff, issued from inside an agent subgraph, navigates to a node in the parent graph.

options.text: END
None
"support_agent"
Command.PARENT

questions.explanation: Handoff tools in the multiple-agent-subgraphs approach use Command.PARENT to pick which parent-graph node runs next.

questions.title: Why should a handoff tool that updates messages include a ToolMessage with a matching tool_call_id?

options.text: It tells LangGraph which node to run next
It deletes earlier messages to save tokens
It completes the tool call's request-response cycle so the history stays well-formed
It lets the handoff skip the checkpointer

questions.explanation: An LLM expects a response to every tool call it makes, and without the ToolMessage the conversation history becomes malformed. Routing is done by Command, not by the message.

questions.title: Why does the transfer_to_sales example pass only [last_ai_message, transfer_message] instead of the whole subagent conversation?

options.text: LangGraph rejects message lists longer than two
The full history can confuse the receiving agent with irrelevant reasoning and costs more tokens; summarize in the ToolMessage if more context is needed
Checkpoints cannot store more than two messages
The receiving agent cannot read long ToolMessage content

questions.explanation: Passing only the handoff pair keeps the parent context focused on high-level coordination. The docs suggest summarizing the subagent's work in the ToolMessage if the receiver needs more.

questions.title: Which handoffs implementation approach do the docs recommend for most use cases because it is simpler?

options.text: Multiple agent subgraphs using Command.PARENT
A single agent with middleware that changes its prompt and tools based on state
A router that fans out with Send
A skills agent using load_skill

questions.explanation: The docs recommend a single agent with middleware for most handoffs. Use subgraphs only when you need bespoke agent implementations, such as a node that is itself a complex graph.

questions.title: What does this middleware do on every model call?

options.text: It summarizes the message history before each call
It routes execution to a separate agent node
It reads current_step from state and overrides the system prompt and tools for that step
It persists current_step to the checkpointer

questions.explanation: In the single-agent handoff approach, middleware intercepts each model call and applies a step-specific prompt and tool set. Tools change current_step to trigger the transition.

questions.title: When does this routing function end the graph?

options.text: When the last message is an AIMessage with no tool calls, meaning the agent finished without a handoff
Whenever active_agent is unset
After exactly one agent turn
When the last message is a ToolMessage

questions.explanation: An AIMessage without tool calls is a final reply to the user, so the graph ends. Otherwise the function routes to the active agent, which keeps handoffs flowing.

questions.title: Which LangGraph primitive does the router pattern use to fan out to several specialized agents in parallel?

options.text: Send
Command.PARENT
interrupt
add_edge

questions.explanation: Router docs use Send for parallel fan-out and Command for routing to a single agent.

questions.title: What does this router function do?

options.text: It routes to a single agent chosen by the classifier
It runs the classified agents one after another
It only updates the state without routing
It fans out in parallel to each classified agent with its own sub-query

questions.explanation: Returning a list of Send objects dispatches to every selected agent in parallel, each with its own input. Results are then synthesized.

questions.title: Which statements correctly distinguish a router from a supervisor (subagents pattern)?

options.text: A router is typically a dedicated routing step, such as one LLM call or rule-based logic, that classifies input and dispatches
A supervisor is a full agent that keeps conversation context and decides which subagents to call across multiple turns
A router normally keeps multi-turn history and orchestrates multi-step workflows itself
A router fits clear input categories and lightweight classification, while a supervisor fits flexible conversation-aware orchestration

questions.explanation: The router is usually a stateless preprocessing step and does not maintain ongoing conversation state. That multi-turn orchestration is the supervisor's job.

questions.title: What can a node in a custom LangGraph workflow be?

options.text: Only a compiled agent
A simple function, an LLM call, or an entire agent with tools
Only a deterministic function
Only another StateGraph

questions.explanation: Custom workflows mix deterministic logic and agentic behavior, and you can even embed other multi-agent patterns as a single node.

questions.title: The parent graph and the subgraph share state keys. Fill the blank to add the subgraph as a node.
questions.codeSnippet:
subgraph = subgraph_builder.compile()

builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("node_1", ______)
builder.add_edge(START, "node_1")
graph = builder.compile()

options.text: subgraph_builder
subgraph.invoke
subgraph
"subgraph"

questions.explanation: With shared state keys you pass the compiled subgraph directly to add_node and need no wrapper function. The uncompiled builder is not a runnable node.

questions.title: A parent graph and a subgraph have different state schemas with no shared keys, for example to keep a private message history per agent. How should the subgraph be used?

options.text: Call it inside a node function that maps parent state to subgraph input and the result back
Pass it directly to add_node
Merge both schemas into a single TypedDict
Compile it with checkpointer=False

questions.explanation: Different schemas need a wrapper node that transforms state in both directions. Passing the subgraph directly works only when the schemas share keys.

questions.title: What is the consequence of compiling a subgraph with checkpointer=False?

options.text: It remembers earlier calls across the same thread
Each invocation inherits the parent's checkpointer for interrupts
get_state(subgraphs=True) shows its accumulated state
It runs like a plain function call with no interrupts or durable execution, so a crash means re-running from the start

questions.explanation: False means stateless: no checkpointing, so no interrupt() and no recovery after a crash. The default None keeps per-invocation checkpointing, and True gives per-thread memory.
